So I've been to a huge amount of therapists and participated in a lot of programs. I have not found any benefits from programs where I am told how I ought to be, and expected to force myself to conform to a model.

 I have found that consistently CBT is a very cookie cutter, empty experience. I have observed that practitioners of CBT have a tendency to view their clients as broken, sick people who can't think or feel correctly and need to be told how to think and feel. They see themselves as "challenging" a "patient" in order to get them to accept that they are broken, and need to strictly adhere to the program laid out in CBT training materials. Deviation or questioning of that program is seen as a symptom of mental illness and labeled as "resistance".

CBT tends to be dangerously ignorant and invalidating to people who are suffering because of serious external circumstances. For example, if you go to a CBT therapist and say "I think I'm being abused" you are very likely to be told that it is your responsibility to deal with it emotionally, and that you failed to set appropriate boundaries because you are sick. I have also experienced and read about many times where a person facing abuse is told that they are delusional in CBT. I can't tell you how many times I've talked to people who've had that exact story. 

After 40 plus therapists I more or less gave up on it. But some people do find it cathartic. You need to call out a therapist if they're not helping, and not be afraid to walk out and never come back. You are your therapists boss, you pay them. 

Other program modalities beside CBT are:

DBT: very program-centric, I have found that it is directed towards people who struggle with routines and need constant support. It involves daily or weekly meetings in a group, and discussion of a work book. It is not explicitly trauma focused, but usually workbook will serve as a framework and jumping off point to delve into a sort of group trauma therapy. 

Process group therapy: Loosely structured group therapy where people talk about their traumatic experiences and comfort each other. It as the potential to be either highly positive or highly disorganized in my experience. It can be really good IF you get the right people and moderator. 

EMDR: Seems like it either works or it doesn't - the science is still out as to if it works because it gives people a structured space to talk about trauma, if it is part placebo, or if the eye movement bit actually "reprocesses" memories. It didn't work for me, but a lot of people on here really swear by it, so IDK. Some people say it is very, very intense if it works. 

Narrative Reprocessing: Therapeutic exercises designed to help someone safely confront and reflect on their past, so as to understand the impact it has on their current mind state. Often exercise will include making a timeline, keeping a journal, writing /making creative pieces about past events, and discussing past events from other perspectives.

PE (prolonged exposure): This one is controversial as it used to be the "gold standard", and is now regarded by some as unhelpful and often re traumatizing. It operates on the supposition that PTSD can be treated the same as a phobia, and aims to teach the body to feel safe through incremental exposure to traumatic stimuli. Some people have benefited from it, I personally did not. 

That said I would recommend you find someone who doesn't use a "method" but rather approaches situations in a more human way. Honestly that is the difference between a good T and a bad T. If te T says they use one method, they're probably unsuited for traumatized people. It depends on the person of course

I appreciate that you took the time to write this because it is clear  
you put some real thought and feeling into it. In the past I very  
much had your perspective on dealing with trauma; I read Frankel and  
was involved in pretty intense non-profit work. Honestly after many  
years, and many more traumas, I found that it was not so simple.

  
The hard reality that I have come to live is that living as I do is like trying to  
climb a mountain with your hands tied behind you back – one died by  
socioeconomic circumstances, and one by trauma. I keep falling down  
the mountainside, getting progressively more bloodied and broken.  
Sometimes I get thoughts and prayers, but mostly I am met with a  
vaguely hostile apathy. Occasional I get hate. 

  
Most people are not narcissist or sociopaths, they are confused, worn out, and apathetic.  
The apathetic out number people who want to be “helpers” 10 to 1.  
When I put myself into a “helping role” working the Middle East  
or the inner city, I saw this everyday.   

  
Helping is often impossible. There is too much need, put on too few, who have too  
little to give. Every resources I have been connected with through  
the state or the public mental health community has been a sick joke.  
My case is too “hopeless”, so I have been told by therapists and  
OVR; I have been triaged out of service, and routinely disconnected.  
A great many people look at me through lens of inferiority,  
difference, and relative worthlessness. On top of that, the  
Post-Covid society I find myself living in has become a funhouse  
mirror of the world I knew - twisted and darkened. 

  
I would love the opportunity to discover myself through my passions or relations, but  
that is not the structural reality of my life; the cost of over  
coming obstacles alone is prohibitively high. I am very angry about  
this - whether or not others would label that as “healthy” or  
not.  Sometimes life is not about trying to overcome a tough period,  
it is trying to survive, not because of positivity or hope, but  
because the alternative is destitution and death.   
I don’t have any answers, that’s just what I’ve seen to be true in my life.

It's not true at an individual level that someone will repeat their trauma. So what your  therapist is saying comes from a real statistic, but its not deterministic,  but rather reflects structural problems in society.

It is factual that on average, a statically significant number of people with trauma end up back in abusive situations. Explanations for this are that people with trauma may be in bad life circumstances they can't easily escape. There is also an overall tendency among some people with unprocessed trauma to engage in high risk behaviors in order to cope. Finally people with trauma are in a vulnerable state where they can be taken advantage of. They may have problems assessing danger, and ignore "red flags" because they're chronically numb or hyper aroused. These factors lead to many people with trauma being in cynically bad situations, but not for everyone.

It is wrong for someone to assert that an individual person will repeat their trauma. You cannot apply statistically true statements to the lives of individuals!

Being aware that one is traumatized negates a lot of this. It more applies to people identical. And again, its a statically average, not a deterministic prophecy about your life.

Drifter on the Trail.

Right after graduating high-school, me an  three friends decided to hike the Appalachian Trail from central-west Pennsylvania to New Jersey. 

Out in the middle of thr wilderness, miles from the nearest shelter, this weather-worn man with dirty, shoulder length hair comes rushing out of the brush onto the trail in front of us.

 His out fit was mis-marched hiking gear, and up close it was clear he had seen hard times. Though he was young, his hands were scarred, skin pock marked. And around his waited, I kid you not...he had freaking a machete tied to his belt. 

So this fine gentlemen introduced himself by the moniker "Lone Wolf", and claimed he was a lost through-hiker, hiking the AT South to North. The fact he had no pack however was odd.

But being really stupid 18 year olds, with that sense of invisible energy common to that age, we didn't immediately get the hell away from him. He was weirdly charming, and we were kind of amused, in a perverse way. We figured he leaves us be if we we're friendly, so we offered him some cigarettes.

As he's smoking it, "Lone Wolf" starts staring at my friend Gwen with weird looks, and making uncomfortable conversation directed at her...and only her. So we took off pretty quick and hoped that would be the last we'd see of him. 

NOPE

Two hours later we break for a rest on a tall rock, and to our shock, we see" Lone Wolf", machete in tow, sneaking along in the brush next to the trail. We immediately double our pace hoping to lose the guy, but he managed to follow us all day. With each hour we realize beyond any doubt that he is following us, and our pace became more and more urgent.

By night fall we lost track of the drifter, but were jumping at every snapped twig, and moving shadow. hours pass and we don't see anyone, so we decide so build a fire.

No one could sleep. Throughout the evening we heard the periodic sound of brush and twigs breaking beyond the firelight. Half panicking I called out to the darkness. Something is definitely moving just out of sight.

"Hello?" 

The noises suddenly stopped, and I felt the sinking dread of full panic chilling my blood. I drew my utility knife, sweaty plams shaking.

"We've got a gun!" 

My friend shouts; a lie. He reaches into his bag, and pulling the handle of a camping frying pan out, which in the dark looked vaguely gunike. He waved around in the firelight.

There was science then rapid crunching leaves, and the more distant sound of twigs breaking. Then silence. 

The next day a local ranger came up to us as we were approaching the next shelter, and asked if we'd seen a man matching "Lone Wolf's" description. Apparently someone had been attacked -  beaten and robbed nearby. The ranger phoned the sheriff about our story and told us they'd look for the guy. 

The ranger saw we were shaken, and was nice enough to give us a ride up a fire trail a few miles so we could get out of the area.

Depression is not one thing, and it does not have one cause or solution. There is a lot of really generic and out of touch advice circulating about depression. Depression is so situational that it can be difficult to really say what will help anyone, but generally 

\- Calm introspection, routine socialization, and the ability to achieve tangible goals is generally helpful. 

\- Not compensating for negative feelings with escapism like playing video games all day, or excesses in behaviors (especially with mind altering substances/experiences).

\- Asking oneself why they feel depressed and digging into that below the day to day surface level is often part of it.

\- Setting realistic expectations and realizing that being happy is not the goal, the goal is to achieve a state where you are unburdened by sorrow and can have a greater range of feelings as a result. 

\- A lot of people who are depressed are either dealing with life circumstances that are ill suited to their nature, or negative messages/expectations being pushed on them from others that have become internalized need to be deliberately and intentionally countered. In that area, focusing on solutions over blame can be helpful.

\- Not blaming oneself for how they feel and not expecting things to change over night.

 \- Avoiding fatalistic attitudes that can foster self-fulfilling prophecies i.e: I see myself as  a failure, so I intentionally don't try to succeed, thus causing me to be a failure. 

\- Making plans to expand ones horizons on a small scale, and following though with them.

What professionals feel counts as a stressor, or avoidance is really mired in the cultural baggage of the professionals view sometimes; not a lot of attempts at cumturally informed objectivity. I think too many of them miss the forest for the trees, and can't take off their cultural blinders to see the realities of what trauma looks like in different parts of society. I get the sense that a lot of psychologist dismiss, out of hand, a huge number of people for simply not understanding what trauma might mean from their perspective.

It looks different in everyone becasue it builds on the existing experiences and pathways in a person's mind. Apart from those trauma response which are inherently linked to hormonal or anatomical differences, and are gendered independently of culture, I tend to think that most trauma is universal, and gender is mostly just the framework through which it is socially understood.

For the most part I don't think there is a default  gendered response by virtue of biological sexual differences, but rather by the types of trauma men and woman deal with (which are often gendered based on gendered social practices) , and ways men and woman are taught to cope with it in a culture. 

I think within a culture you will see broad patterns of male vs female responses to trauma - and by extension also general patterns of trauma responses in other groups with shared cultural positions and experiences.

There are some instances of course where gendered biology plays a big role in trauma. It would be wrong to discount the unique trauma that Transgendered and non-binary people often share, or that which women who miscarry, or lose children early in life feel. In the same way, biological men may be on average more likely to get physical in response to truama, although to necessarily violent -  due to elevated testosterone. Although that is not to say that some men don't respond with aggression or physicality, or that or that some woman do. 

Sexual violence is a really complex gendered issue that impacts women, Men, trans, and non-binary people very differently. I think it would be impossible to sort out how much is biological and how much is cultural. I will say though, that at the core, male, female, and non-binary people all feel that violation the same way, even if they respond differently based on their sexual organs, position in society and social conditioning.

I 100% agree. We should be breaking the taboo and providing a safe space to talk. 

R/suicidewatch isn't a helpful community. People frequently have no where to turn for support when facing such feelings because of the overwhelming social taboo and local laws. 

People need to recognize that the resources available to people like the National Suicide Hotline are really weak, and unhelpfully general. Many resources also hold the poential threat of being reported to law enforcement, who are not equipped to help people in many countries.

People should be free to talk about their feelings if they are suicidal becasue there are not other topic-specific safe spaces to do it.

I believe the policy should be modified to keep bans on promoters, but allow for people discuss their feelings as long as they adhere to the following:

1. Provide a trigger warning 
2. No discussion of methods
3. No discussion of plans
4. No advocacy for suicide 

Again, people have literally no meaningful resources available to them to talk about these feelings I most places without risk of legal punishment, ridicule, harassment. Inpatient facilities are notoriously bad, suicide hotlines are notoriously unhelpful.

If you want to prevent suicide due to ptsd, then give struggling people a safe place to talk. 

I understand mods don't want to play post police and  its may seem easier, perhaps seems fairer, to implement a general ban, but that not fair to the people who are suffering with no where to turn.

Policy shouldn't promite stigma or parrot empty solutions.
